"Corrupt" describes something — or someone — that has been spoiled, tainted, or made bad from a state that was once good, pure, honest, or properly functioning. Think of it like fruit going rotten: a fresh apple is wholesome and intact, but a rotten one has been corrupted — its original good nature has been ruined from within. This idea of degradation from something better is the thread that runs through every use of this word.
The Most Common Use: Morally Corrupt People

When we call a person corrupt, we mean they are dishonest and willing to abuse their power or position for personal gain — usually through bribery, fraud, deception, or favoritism.

A corrupt person doesn't follow the rules they are supposed to uphold. Instead, they secretly bend or break those rules to benefit themselves or someone close to them. A corrupt politician accepts money (a bribe) in exchange for passing laws that benefit the person paying. A corrupt judge makes rulings not based on the law, but based on who paid them more. A corrupt police officer allows criminals to go free in exchange for money. A corrupt official gives government contracts to their friends and family instead of the most qualified candidates — practices known as nepotism and cronyism.

What makes this especially serious is that corrupt people are almost always in positions of trust. A judge is supposed to be fair. A police officer is supposed to protect the public. A politician is supposed to serve the people. When someone in such a position is corrupt, they are betraying the very trust that was placed in them — and that betrayal causes real harm to everyone who depended on them to be honest.

Corrupt also implies secrecy. A corrupt person rarely announces their dishonesty. They wear a mask of legitimacy and honesty on the outside while doing wrong in secret. This hidden nature is part of what makes corruption so dangerous — by the time it is discovered, the damage is often already deep.

"Corrupt" doesn't only describe individuals. Entire organizations, governments, police forces, courts, or companies can be called corrupt.

When a system is corrupt, dishonesty, bribery, and abuse of power aren't acts committed by just one bad person — they are widespread and deeply built into how the whole system operates. Honest behavior has become the exception, not the norm. For example, saying "the country's judicial system is corrupt" means that bribery, political pressure, and favoritism are so common in the courts that getting a fair, honest ruling is nearly impossible.

Something or someone doesn't have to be completely corrupt. You might say someone is "mildly corrupt," meaning there is some dishonesty but it isn't all-consuming. On the other hand, "deeply corrupt" or "thoroughly corrupt" means dishonesty has taken over so completely that there is almost nothing honest or good left.
The Technical Meaning: Corrupt Data or Files

In computing and technology, "corrupt" takes on a related but more literal meaning. A corrupt file or corrupt data is one that has been damaged or altered in a way that makes it broken, incomplete, or unreadable — it no longer works as it should.

Just as a morally corrupt person has deviated from proper, honest behavior, a corrupt file has deviated from its proper, intact state. For example: "The document was corrupt, so I couldn't open it" means the file was somehow damaged — perhaps during saving, during a transfer, or by a virus — and is no longer functioning correctly.
The Literary and Historical Meaning: Corrupt Texts

In literature and history, scholars sometimes refer to a corrupt text or a corrupt manuscript. This means a written document — often an ancient one — that has accumulated errors over time through repeated hand-copying, mistranslation, or deliberate alteration, so that it no longer accurately reflects the original. A scholar might note: "This version of the ancient poem is corrupt because several lines were changed or lost over centuries of copying."
The Single Thread Running Through All Meanings

No matter which sense you encounter, "corrupt" always points to the same fundamental idea: something that was once good, pure, whole, honest, or properly functioning has been damaged, tainted, or degraded — and is now in a worse state. A corrupt person was (or should be) honest, but is now dishonest. A corrupt system was (or should be) fair, but is now unjust. A corrupt file was once whole, but is now broken. A corrupt text was once accurate, but is now distorted.

Corruption implies a process, not just a fixed condition. The word suggests that something changed for the worse — it wasn't always this way. This is why we say someone "became corrupt" or that a file "got corrupted." There is always a before and an after.

Corruption also tends to happen from the inside. Just as fruit rots from within, corruption usually describes degradation that originates internally — the very person who should be upholding standards is the one destroying them; the very data that made a file functional is the data that has become scrambled.

And "corrupt" is always negative, without exception. There is no positive or neutral use of this word. Calling something or someone corrupt is always a criticism or a statement of damage.

The most important antonym of corrupt is incorruptible — describing a person who cannot be bribed, manipulated, or made dishonest, no matter the pressure or temptation they face. An incorruptible judge always follows the law fairly, regardless of who offers money or influence. This quality is considered one of the highest moral virtues a person in power can possess. Other antonyms include honest, upright, righteous, and clean in the moral sense, and intact or undamaged in the technical sense.

In the moral sense, corrupt is close in meaning to crooked, dishonest, fraudulent, and venal (venal specifically suggests being motivated by money and willing to do anything for it — it is a particularly sharp synonym). In the technical or data sense, it is similar to damaged, broken, and faulty.
